problems.title: The result comparator loses semantic distinctions and rejects correct empty results
problems.source_location: Appendices C–D, PDF p. 25; released PostgreSQL utility preprocess_results, lines 10–29, and ex_baselines, lines 92–134.
claim: Appendices C–D, PDF p. 25, describe functional SQL evaluation. The released PostgreSQL utility preprocess_results, lines 10–29, and ex_base, lines 86–132, discard duplicates/time-of-day and reject empty answers. Required ordering is also not enforced by set comparison.
analysis: Set comparison equates the row sequences \(((1),(1))\) and \(((1))\), losing multiplicity and any required order. Rejecting either empty list rejects two identical valid empty answers. Formatting timestamps as dates equates same-day values \(22\) hours apart. These are distinct valid-answer contracts that a general semantic comparator must preserve; their frequency in the final task tests is unknown.

problems.title: Removing DISTINCT with text operations changes valid SQL values and query structure
problems.source_location: Released PostgreSQL utility remove_distinct, lines 32–61; retained conference and current-source versions.
claim: The conference remove_distinct, lines 32–61 of the PostgreSQL utility, splits each complete SQL string on whitespace, removes tokens equal to distinct, and joins the remainder with single spaces. The current version instead uses a case-insensitive regular expression replacing every whole-word occurrence of DISTINCT with an empty string. The authors’ README explicitly announces an evaluation-code update to this function on \(8\) January 2026.
analysis: The current helper applies a case-insensitive whole-word regular expression to the entire SQL string. Thus the valid statement SELECT 'DISTINCT' AS value is changed into SELECT '' AS value. This changes a string value, rather than a SQL keyword. The former split/join behavior that collapsed double spaces or moved a statement into a line comment has been fixed and is excluded from the current defect. Actual benchmark incidence remains unknown.

problems.title: The denominator and stopping rule for Table 4’s average tries require clarification
problems.source_location: Section 4, PDF p. 5; Section 6.4, Table 4, PDF p. 9.
claim: Section 4, PDF p. 5, describes SIX-GYM as containing approximately \(3301\) generated training instances. Section 6.4 and Table 4, p. 9, compare trajectory generation on SIX-GYM. The Reject + f-Plan row has at most five tries, \(2560\) successful trajectories, and an average of \(1.7\) tries. The same table values remain in arXiv v4. The table itself does not explicitly specify its average’s denominator.

Suppose average tries means the mean over all \(3301\) tasks; each successfully solved task consumes at least one try; and each final failure exhausts all five allowed tries. These are an explicit interpretation being tested, not assumptions asserted as supported facts about the run.
analysis: Assume the mean covers all \(3301\) tasks, every one of \(2560\) successes takes at least one try, and each of \(741\) failures exhausts five tries. The mean must then be at least \((2560+5\cdot741)/3301\approx1.89791\), inconsistent with \(1.7\). A success-only denominator, early aborts or another averaging unit removes this contradiction. The table does not establish the assumptions, so no incorrect entry or replacement value is asserted.
result: Reporting ambiguity requiring denominator/stopping-rule evidence; no incorrect table entry or replacement number is established.
assumptions: The finding is restricted to the identified paper version and identified released component; published experiment provenance is not inferred from public code alone.
repair: Specify the averaging unit, total attempts, success count and terminal-failure behavior.
problems.impact_rationale: The mechanism is plausible, but the evidence needed to establish the claimed experimental or historical effect is missing; the item remains unresolved.
